title: Why Cebreros tastes the way it does

lede.text: Some of Cebreros's vines grow above 1,000 m, on granite slopes that face south. Garnacha Tinta gives wines high in alcohol there, yet altitude and climate keep them fresh.

chapters.title: Between two rivers, under Gredos
paras: The vineyards lie in the south-east of the province of Ávila, in an area of 1663.16 km2. They sit between the basins of the Alberche and the Tiétar, two tributaries of the Tajo. The eastern massif of the Sierra de Gredos is the ridge that separates the two basins.

The foothills of Gredos begin at Cerro Guisando, 1,303 m high, in El Tiemblo. Further west a line of peaks rises to around 2000 m. The relief is generally rough but without very sharp forms. Tall hills with steep slopes rise among large flat-bottomed valleys called navas.

Vines grow mainly on the south-facing slopes of the hills on the left bank of the valley. The Tiétar valley is gentler than the Alberche, but there is still a big drop from the peaks to its river, which runs at 500 m. Growers have picked south and south-east slopes for centuries, and some plots lie above 1,000 m.

chapters.title: Hot and dry, but with altitude
paras: The climate is Mediterranean with a continental touch. Summers are long and hot, and they are dry. Winters are relatively short and not very cold. Rain falls mostly in autumn and winter, though spring rain can be heavy in the Tiétar valley. June to September are the driest months. On the Gredos peaks the climate is mountain: winters are very cold and summers cool, with heavy rain all year.
The vineyards average 12 to 15°C a year. July and August average 23.3 to 25.8°C, and January and December 5.0 to 8.6°C. The frost-free period runs from 215 days in the north to 275 in the south.
Yearly rainfall in the vineyards is 400 to 800 mm. In the south-west some areas pass 1000 mm.

The local microclimate is more moderate than the rest of Castilla y León and cooler than the lands to the south and east. The lack of rain in summer and early autumn assures healthy, high-quality harvests. The altitude gives the grapes very good acidity, and that brings freshness and liveliness to the wine.

chapters.title: Granite, sand and old vines
paras: Granite is the mark of the zone, and most of the vineyards stand on it. It is an acid rock, formed by the slow solidification of magma rich in silica long ago, in the Carboniferous and Permian. Some vines also grow on schist and on recent deposits.
The soils are mostly sandy loam. They are slightly acid and low in organic matter. Granite with sandy loam gives the wines finesse and an elegant feel in the mouth.

Phylloxera reached the province of Ávila only in 1909, one of the last areas of the Iberian peninsula to be hit. The pest spread slowly in sandy soil, so some vines stood on their own roots until the 1960s.

Today 94% of the vines are over 50 years old and 37% are over 80. Spacing is wide, generally more than 2.5 x 2.5 metres, at 1,600 vines per hectare. This wide spacing, with low rain and soils poor in organic matter, gives very small crops of well-balanced grapes.

chapters.title: Two grapes, and barrels of oak
paras: Only two grapes lead the wines. Rosés and reds are at least 95% Garnacha Tinta, with Garnacha Tintorera and Tempranillo allowed as secondary reds. White wine is made only from Albillo Real. It is local to the area and different from Albillo Mayor, which is typical of other parts of Castilla y León. Its whites are complex and tasty. They are lively and age well in barrel.

Garnacha Tinta gives a high alcohol, yet altitude and climate keep the wine fresh. All the wines share a high alcohol and a high, balanced acidity. They live long, the reds above all, which have a high potential for keeping. Every colour comes both young and aged.

Barrel ageing changes the wines. Whites become more unctuous and fuller, with riper fruit and a hint of wood. Rosés and reds gain softness and persistence. Reds show toast and spice next to the fruit. Ageing is in oak barrels, and the clock starts on 1 November of the harvest year.

Yields are capped at 8,000 kg per hectare, and no more than 56.00 hl per hectare. Only mechanical systems that do not tear the solid parts of the bunch may extract the must. No more than 70 litres of wine may come from 100 kg of grapes. In some years, after a reasoned technical report, yields may rise by up to 15% and the limit to 74 litres of wine per 100 kg.

terms.text: The wine ferments and rests on its lees in oak barrels.
All the grapes come from one plot or from neighbouring plots, with no herbicides and a soil analysis by the producer.
All the grapes come from one named municipality.
